text: Grover's algorithm and the QFT run entirely on the quantum processor, start to finish. Variational algorithms are different: they deliberately split the work between a quantum circuit and a classical optimizer, running back and forth between the two until the result converges.

A variational algorithm has four moving parts. An ansatz — a parameterized circuit like RY of theta on |0>, whose parameters get tuned. An objective operator — a Hamiltonian H whose expectation value you want to minimize. Quantum evaluation — run the ansatz through an Estimator primitive to measure that expectation value. And a classical update — an optimizer proposes new parameters based on what was measured. Steps three and four repeat until the optimizer converges.

VQE and COBYLA come from the separate qiskit-algorithms package, while StatevectorEstimator is a core qiskit primitive used to evaluate expectation values during simulation. VQE was originally developed for quantum chemistry, where the minimum achievable expectation value is a molecule's ground-state energy. QAOA applies the same hybrid-loop structure to combinatorial optimization.

To make this concrete, use a deliberately simplified toy Hamiltonian: 0.5 times Z plus 0.3 times X, with ansatz RY of theta on |0>. The expectation value has a clean closed form: 0.5 cosine theta plus 0.3 sine theta. At theta equals zero, that's 0.5. At pi over 2, it's 0.3. At pi, negative 0.5. Notice it isn't monotonically decreasing — it rises slightly before it falls. The true minimum is negative 0.583095, at theta of roughly 3.68 radians — none of those sampled points come close.

COBYLA is a gradient-free optimizer — it doesn't need the derivative of the expectation value, only the ability to evaluate it at chosen points: try one, see whether the value went up or down, adjust, repeat. This matters because on real hardware you cannot get an exact derivative for free — every measurement is already a noisy, finite-shot estimate, and computing a true gradient would mean extra, separate measurements at shifted parameters.

Next lesson is a lab where you run the real Grover circuit yourself and confirm its exact predicted result, then hand-evaluate this toy VQE landscape at points of your own choosing — building real intuition for what an optimizer does with nothing but point evaluations.
